compliance.desc: Same profile as the other LAO cuts.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Niche EOR/drilling-fluid intermediate — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Internal olefins carry no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: Historical adulteration/poisoning risk when illegally substituted for pharmaceutical glycerin
compliance.name: A misuse/fraud concern in pharma supply chains, not a restriction on legitimate industrial use
compliance.desc: Diethylene glycol has been implicated in a number of serious poisoning incidents internationally when criminally substituted for glycerin in pharmaceutical syrups; this is a supply-chain integrity and fraud-prevention issue relevant to pharma-adjacent buyers specifically, not a restriction on its legitimate industrial (antifreeze, plasticizer, solvent) uses.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard gas-dehydration/industrial glycol — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Triethylene glycol carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: Occupational exposure limits apply; no product-level restriction
compliance.name: Standard industrial hygiene framework, not a use restriction
compliance.desc: Vinyl acetate monomer is subject to established occupational exposure limits reflecting its respiratory irritant properties, but carries no restriction on manufacture or use.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard nylon 6 feedstock — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Caprolactam carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: N2O byproduct is a potent greenhouse gas subject to climate-policy scrutiny
compliance.name: A genuine, decades-long environmental compliance consideration for producers
compliance.desc: The nitric-acid oxidation step in adipic acid manufacture generates nitrous oxide (N2O), a greenhouse gas roughly 300x more potent than CO2 over 100 years; this has driven voluntary and regulatory abatement requirements at production facilities for decades (including coverage under the EU Emissions Trading System) — a real, producer-level environmental compliance consideration rather than a restriction on the product itself.

compliance.flag: Indirect exposure to phthalate-plasticizer regulatory scrutiny via downstream esters
compliance.name: The anhydride itself is not the regulated substance
compliance.desc: Phthalic anhydride is the feedstock for phthalate ester plasticizers (some of which face EU/US restrictions in child-contact applications), but the anhydride itself is not a regulated phthalate ester and carries no direct restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard UPR/BDO feedstock — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Maleic anhydride carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: Historical food-adulteration scandal shaped strict food-contact regulation, not a restriction on legitimate resin use
compliance.name: 2008 milk-adulteration crisis involved criminal misuse, not legitimate industrial melamine
compliance.desc: The 2008 Chinese infant-formula adulteration crisis involved criminal addition of industrial melamine to food products to falsify protein content — a fraud/food-safety event that led to strict international food-contact migration limits for melamine resin tableware, but does not restrict legitimate industrial melamine resin manufacture for laminates and coatings.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard food-grade organic acid — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Fumaric acid carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified

compliance.desc: Gluconic acid carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.desc: Liquid nitrogen carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard industrial gas — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Liquid oxygen carries no major known regulatory restriction beyond standard oxidizer handling.

compliance.flag: Favored, mandated low-GWP refrigerant under EU F-Gas and MAC Directive rules
compliance.name: A genuinely positive regulatory position, not a risk
compliance.desc: R-1234yf is the EU-mandated replacement refrigerant for new vehicle air conditioning (required since 2017 under the Mobile Air Conditioning Directive) precisely because of its very low global warming potential — its regulatory position is favorable, not a compliance risk.

compliance.flag: Kigali Amendment/EU F-Gas Regulation phase-down; already banned in new vehicle AC
compliance.name: An active, binding phase-down already reducing legal supply
compliance.desc: R-134a is a high-GWP HFC subject to binding phase-down under both the Montreal Protocol's Kigali Amendment and the EU F-Gas Regulation's shrinking HFC quota system, and has already been banned in new-vehicle air conditioning systems in the EU since 2017 — this is an active, structural supply reduction, not a future risk.

compliance.flag: Favored transitional lower-GWP HFC under EU F-Gas quota rules
compliance.name: Better-positioned than R-134a/R-410A, but still an HFC subject to long-term phase-down
compliance.desc: R-32's lower GWP than R-134a or R-410A makes it a favored transitional refrigerant under the EU F-Gas quota system, though as an HFC it remains subject to the same long-term Kigali Amendment phase-down trajectory as other HFCs, just later in the schedule.

compliance.flag: Kigali Amendment/EU F-Gas Regulation phase-down affects this HFC blend
compliance.name: An active, binding phase-down already reducing legal supply
compliance.desc: As an HFC blend, R-410A is subject to the same binding Kigali Amendment/EU F-Gas phase-down as R-134a, with HVAC manufacturers increasingly shifting toward R-32 or newer HFO blends (e.g. R-454B) in new equipment.

compliance.flag: Favored natural, ultra-low-GWP refrigerant/process gas under current regulatory trends
compliance.name: A genuinely positive regulatory position where used as a refrigerant
compliance.desc: CO2 is treated as a natural refrigerant with negligible GWP under F-Gas frameworks, giving it a favorable long-term regulatory position relative to synthetic HFC/HFO refrigerants; as an industrial process gas more broadly, it carries no restriction.

compliance.flag: Seveso III major-accident-hazard regulation applies to bulk hydrogen storage
compliance.name: Facility-level safety regulation, not a product restriction
compliance.desc: Bulk hydrogen storage above threshold quantities triggers Seveso III major-accident-hazard obligations for the storing facility, a standard safety framework rather than a restriction on hydrogen itself.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: EU-authorized feed amino acid — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: L-lysine is an established, EU-authorized feed additive under Regulation 1831/2003 with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: EU-authorized feed amino acid — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: DL-methionine is an established, EU-authorized feed additive with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: EU-authorized feed amino acid — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: L-threonine is an established, EU-authorized feed additive with no known compliance concern.

compliance.name: EU-authorized feed vitamin — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Feed-grade vitamin D3 is an established, EU-authorized feed additive with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: EU-authorized feed vitamin — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Feed-grade vitamin E is an established, EU-authorized feed additive with no known compliance concern.

compliance.name: GRAS food/pharma-grade vitamin — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Niacinamide (vitamin B3) is a generally-recognized-as-safe, widely authorized food and pharmaceutical ingredient with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: GRAS food additive (E420) — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Sorbitol is an established, generally-recognized-as-safe food additive (E420) with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: GRAS food ingredient — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Maltodextrin is an established, generally-recognized-as-safe food ingredient with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: EU REACH diisocyanate authorization/training requirement (in force since Aug 2023)
compliance.name: Industrial and professional users must complete mandatory safety training
compliance.desc: Since this thickener is built on an MDI backbone, it falls under the same EU REACH diisocyanate training requirement covering industrial and professional users of MDI-containing products.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: GRAS food/industrial biopolymer — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Xanthan gum is a generally-recognized-as-safe, widely authorized thickener with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified

compliance.desc: Hydroxyethyl cellulose carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard acrylic thickener — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Carbomer carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Established cationic cellulose conditioning polymer — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Polyquaternium-10 is a widely used, established cosmetic ingredient with no known compliance concern.

compliance.flag: Persistence/heavy-metal-remobilization concern drives EU eco-label discouragement
compliance.name: A real, long-standing environmental concern shaping formulation choices
compliance.desc: EDTA is poorly biodegradable and can remobilize heavy metals bound in sediment, a long-recognized environmental concern; several EU eco-label schemes discourage or restrict EDTA in detergents and cleaning products, driving real substitution toward readily biodegradable chelants like GLDA and MGDA.

compliance.flag: Favored as a readily biodegradable EDTA replacement
compliance.name: A genuinely positive environmental/regulatory position
compliance.desc: GLDA was specifically developed and is marketed as a readily biodegradable alternative to EDTA, directly benefiting from the environmental concerns driving EDTA substitution.

compliance.flag: Favored as a readily biodegradable EDTA replacement
compliance.name: A genuinely positive environmental/regulatory position
compliance.desc: Same favorable positioning as GLDA — MGDA is marketed as a readily biodegradable EDTA alternative.

compliance.flag: EU Biocidal Products Regulation active-substance status, subject to periodic renewal review
compliance.name: An approved but periodically re-reviewed biocide, plus known sensitization potential
compliance.desc: Glutaraldehyde is an approved active substance under the EU Biocidal Products Regulation for specific product types, subject to the normal periodic renewal review process, and is also a recognized skin/respiratory sensitizer requiring appropriate occupational handling precautions.

compliance.flag: EU Cosmetics Regulation sets a maximum concentration limit (1%)
compliance.name: A settled, well-established limit rather than an emerging risk
compliance.desc: Phenoxyethanol is an approved cosmetic preservative under EU Cosmetics Regulation Annex V with a defined 1% maximum concentration limit — a long-settled compliance framework, not an active or emerging concern.

compliance.flag: EU Biocidal Products Regulation active-substance review; sensitization scrutiny
compliance.name: Under the same regulatory review track as other isothiazolinones, less severely restricted than MIT
compliance.desc: BIT is under EU Biocidal Products Regulation active-substance review like other isothiazolinones and carries sensitization considerations, but has not faced the severe leave-on-cosmetics ban that MIT has — it remains more widely used in industrial (paints, cleaning products) applications.

compliance.flag: EU-banned in leave-on cosmetics (2017); restricted in rinse-off products (2015)
compliance.name: One of the most significant preservative restrictions in recent EU cosmetics regulation
compliance.desc: Following widespread skin-allergy reports, the EU banned methylisothiazolinone (MIT) from leave-on cosmetic products in 2017 and restricted its maximum concentration in rinse-off products in 2015 — a major, well-documented regulatory action that drove substantial reformulation toward alternative preservative systems across the cosmetics industry.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard fragrance ingredient — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Phenylethyl alcohol carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard flavor/fragrance ingredient — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Beta-ionone carries no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: IFRA usage limits due to skin-sensitization potential
compliance.name: A standard, well-established fragrance-industry usage framework
compliance.desc: Citronellol is subject to International Fragrance Association (IFRA) usage limits reflecting its skin-sensitization potential, a normal and long-established part of fragrance formulation compliance rather than an emerging concern.

compliance.flag: EU Cosmetics Regulation mandatory allergen labeling requirement
compliance.name: A real, active labeling obligation above threshold concentration
compliance.desc: Linalool is one of the fragrance substances the EU Cosmetics Regulation requires to be individually declared on product labels when present above a threshold concentration, reflecting its potential to form skin-sensitizing oxidation products on air exposure — a genuine, currently enforced compliance obligation for finished-product labeling.

compliance.flag: Subject to routine EU periodic pesticide-approval renewal review
compliance.name: Standard regulatory process applicable to all approved actives
compliance.desc: Like all EU-approved active substances, azoxystrobin undergoes periodic reapproval review; no non-renewal or ban has occurred, and its patent expiry (2015) is a competitive-market consideration separate from regulatory status.

compliance.flag: EU non-renewal / ban (2020-2021) due to endocrine-disruption and reproductive-toxicity concerns
compliance.name: One of the most significant fungicide bans in recent EU pesticide history
compliance.desc: The EU did not renew mancozeb's approval in 2020-2021, citing endocrine-disrupting properties and reproductive toxicity concerns, resulting in an EU-wide ban on its agricultural use — a major, well-documented regulatory action with real implications for any EU-facing demand for this product.

compliance.flag: Heightened EU regulatory review of the triazole fungicide class
compliance.name: Part of a broader, ongoing EU re-evaluation of triazole fungicides for endocrine-disruption concerns
compliance.desc: Propiconazole belongs to the triazole fungicide class, which has faced heightened EU regulatory scrutiny in recent years over endocrine-disrupting potential; specific approval status should be verified against the current EU pesticide database given the pace of change in this area.

compliance.flag: EU non-renewal / ban (2020) due to genotoxicity and neurodevelopmental toxicity concerns
compliance.name: One of the most significant insecticide bans in recent EU pesticide history
compliance.desc: The EU did not renew chlorpyrifos's approval in 2020, citing genotoxicity and neurodevelopmental toxicity concerns, resulting in an EU-wide ban on its agricultural use — already noted in this product's name, and worth restating as a major, well-documented regulatory action.

compliance.flag: Aquatic toxicity drives buffer-zone and usage restrictions near water bodies
compliance.name: A well-established ecotoxicological consideration for the pyrethroid class generally
compliance.desc: Pyrethroid insecticides including cypermethrin are highly toxic to aquatic invertebrates, which has driven buffer-zone and application-timing restrictions near water bodies in various jurisdictions; this is a well-established usage-stewardship consideration rather than a product ban, and cypermethrin remains a widely used generic active post-patent.

compliance.flag: EU-banned for outdoor use (2018) due to pollinator toxicity
compliance.name: The landmark EU neonicotinoid ban — one of the most significant pesticide regulatory actions globally
compliance.desc: The EU banned outdoor use of imidacloprid and other neonicotinoids in 2018 due to well-documented toxicity to bees and other pollinators — one of the most prominent and consequential pesticide regulatory actions of the past decade, with major implications for EU-facing demand (greenhouse/indoor use remains permitted in some cases).

compliance.flag: Readily biodegradable — meets EU Detergents Regulation threshold
compliance.name: Biodegradability: no compliance concern
compliance.desc: LAS (linear alkylbenzene sulfonate) is readily biodegradable under OECD 301 test methods and meets the ≥60% biodegradation threshold required by EU Detergents Regulation (EC) 648/2004 — this is a settled, well-documented compliance position, not an open risk.

compliance.flag: Mild long-term substitution pressure from bio-based anionics
compliance.name: Structural demand consideration, not an acute risk
compliance.desc: LAS faces gradual, region-specific substitution pressure from bio-based anionic surfactants (notably methyl ester sulfonate, MES, in markets with cheap palm/coconut feedstock, e.g. parts of China and Southeast Asia) in "green" formulation positioning. LAS remains the lowest-cost-per-active anionic surfactant globally and continues to dominate volume; this is a slow structural trend to watch, not a near-term supply risk.

compliance.flag: Readily biodegradable — meets EU Detergents Regulation threshold
compliance.name: Biodegradability: no compliance concern
compliance.desc: Sodium LAS is readily biodegradable under OECD 301 methods and meets the EU Detergents Regulation (EC) 648/2004 biodegradability threshold — a settled compliance position.

compliance.flag: Mild long-term substitution pressure from bio-based anionics
compliance.name: Structural demand consideration, not an acute risk
compliance.desc: As with the acid-paste grade, powder LAS faces slow, region-specific substitution pressure from bio-based anionics (MES) in some green-positioned formulations, but remains the dominant, lowest-cost anionic surfactant for powder detergent globally.

compliance.flag: Readily biodegradable — meets EU Detergents Regulation threshold
compliance.name: Biodegradability: no compliance concern
compliance.desc: Sodium LAS is readily biodegradable and meets the EU Detergents Regulation (EC) 648/2004 threshold — a settled compliance position, applicable equally to this pre-neutralized solution grade.

compliance.flag: Mild long-term substitution pressure from bio-based anionics/SLES blends
compliance.name: Structural demand consideration, not an acute risk
compliance.desc: In liquid detergent formulations specifically, LAS competes with SLES and bio-based anionics for share on cost/mildness/formulation-stability tradeoffs; this is an ongoing formulation choice rather than a supply risk, and LAS remains cost-competitive.

compliance.flag: Readily biodegradable — meets EU Detergents Regulation threshold
compliance.name: Biodegradability: no compliance concern
compliance.desc: Sodium LAS is readily biodegradable and meets the EU Detergents Regulation (EC) 648/2004 threshold — a settled compliance position, applicable equally to this high-concentration slurry grade.

compliance.flag: Mild long-term substitution pressure from bio-based anionics
compliance.name: Structural demand consideration, not an acute risk
compliance.desc: Same slow, region-specific substitution dynamic versus bio-based anionics (MES) as the other LAS grades; LAS remains the dominant, lowest-cost anionic surfactant globally.

compliance.name: Not a drop-in substitution category
compliance.desc: Corrosion inhibitor performance is highly specific to the produced fluid chemistry (CO2/H2S ratio, brine composition, temperature) — a cheaper alternative should be field-trialed before full-scale substitution, not assumed equivalent from a data sheet.

compliance.name: Formulation-specific performance, not universal
compliance.desc: PCE performance varies with cement chemistry and other mix components — a lower-cost alternative should be trial-batched with your specific mix design before switching, similar to the corrosion-inhibitor dynamic elsewhere in this library.

compliance.name: Application-specific testing recommended
compliance.desc: Powder PCE dispersion speed in dry-mix mortars varies by product — trial in the actual dry-mix formulation before full-scale adoption.

compliance.name: Standard latex-industry specification
compliance.desc: Similar to other SB latex applications, residual monomer content should be verified on the certificate of analysis, particularly for interior applications.

compliance.name: Field-specific performance qualification
compliance.desc: Demulsifier performance must be validated via bottle testing on the specific crude/water stream before full deployment — treat as a technical qualification process, not a straightforward commodity purchase.

compliance.name: Structural demand headwind, not a compliance flag
compliance.desc: Lignosulfonate faces ongoing substitution pressure from PCE superplasticizers in higher-performance concrete applications — useful context that a supplier's pricing power here is more limited than in categories without a dominant substitute.

compliance.name: Genuine regulatory-status difference between grades
compliance.desc: The two THPS grade lines have different regulatory status — verify which grade is quoted and whether it's permitted for the intended end-use jurisdiction before purchasing, since this isn't a simple quality-tier difference.

compliance.name: Flammable liquid transport classification
compliance.desc: A real, citable hazmat transport classification affecting freight cost and supplier logistics — verify carrier certification before switching suppliers.

compliance.name: Binding procurement gate
compliance.desc: International Cyanide Management Code certification is increasingly required by mine operators as a condition of supply — a stronger, more concrete compliance gate than most chemicals in this database. Verify current ICMI-signatory status before qualifying a new supplier.

compliance.name: India (Rajasthan/Gujarat) supplies ~80% of global guar
compliance.desc: No meaningful alternative growing region exists at scale. Drought, export restrictions, or logistics disruption in northwest India directly translates to global supply shortage — the 2012 speculative spike is the canonical example.

compliance.name: Guar gum powder is non-hazardous for transport
compliance.desc: Unlike NaCN or MIBC, guar gum powder carries no hazmat classification — a genuine logistics advantage for mining sites with restricted hazmat access.

compliance.name: Standard hazmat classification
compliance.desc: Methanol is both flammable and toxic (methanol poisoning risk) — standard hazmat handling and toxicity documentation should be verified for any new supplier or logistics provider.

compliance.name: Sustainability/carbon-intensity differentiation
compliance.desc: Coal-based MEG (mostly Chinese) carries a higher carbon footprint than naphtha/ethane-route MEG — relevant if the end customer has scope 3 emissions targets on packaging or textile inputs.

compliance.name: Genuine, well-established regulatory concern
compliance.desc: Formaldehyde is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by IARC — occupational exposure limits and emissions regulations (e.g., for composite wood products) are strict and well-established; verify current-spec compliance documentation, this is not a boilerplate flag.

compliance.name: Genuine differentiator for sustainability-driven customers
compliance.desc: PCR-content ABS grades require chain-of-custody certification to substantiate recycled-content claims — verify certification if the end customer needs to report or label recycled content.

compliance.name: Standard corrosive-material handling
compliance.desc: Hydrated lime is caustic and generates significant heat with water — standard PPE and handling protocols apply, verify supplier packaging/documentation meets site requirements.

compliance.name: Standard flammable-liquid hazmat class
compliance.desc: n-Butanol is a Class 3 flammable liquid for transport — standard for solvents in this library, factor into freight/logistics comparison across suppliers.

compliance.name: Pharma/food grade verification required
compliance.desc: USP-grade propylene glycol requires specific purity certification distinct from industrial grade — verify certificates of analysis match the pharmacopeia cited before use in food or pharma formulations.

compliance.name: Distinct grade requirement
compliance.desc: Solar-encapsulant EVA requires UV-stability and optical clarity specifications well beyond general-purpose grades — verify grade matches end use.

compliance.name: Genuine sourcing choice, not a compliance requirement
compliance.desc: Non-GMO or identity-preserved corn starch is available at a premium from all major suppliers for customers with specific labeling requirements — confirm whether this is actually needed before paying the premium by default.

compliance.name: Grade fragmentation drives price, not chemistry
compliance.desc: GCC is sold across a wide range of particle-size and brightness grades at very different price points for chemically identical material — confirm the grade spec matches the application before comparing supplier quotes.

compliance.name: Process route affects purity/cost, not a compliance risk
compliance.desc: ~70% of PCC uses the carbonation process (CO2 + lime); a smaller share uses the hydrochloric acid method for higher-purity grades — useful context when comparing quotes across pharma-grade vs. industrial-grade PCC.

compliance.name: Certification required for potable water use
compliance.desc: Activated carbon used in drinking water treatment must carry NSF/ANSI 61 certification — confirm certification covers the specific grade quoted, not just the supplier's product line generally.

compliance.name: Grade-specific certification needed
compliance.desc: Food- and pharma-grade coconut carbon requires specific certification beyond standard industrial grade — confirm the certified grade matches the intended end use before comparing supplier pricing.

compliance.name: Dual food/industrial grade market
compliance.desc: Ethyl acetate is also approved as a synthetic fruit flavoring agent — food-grade material requires separate certification from industrial solvent grade.

compliance.name: Standard flammable-liquid hazmat class
compliance.desc: n-Butyl acetate is a flammable liquid for transport purposes — standard hazmat handling applies.

compliance.name: Application-specific performance spec
compliance.desc: Bentonite quality is graded by swell index and viscosity performance rather than chemical purity alone — request performance test data, not just an assay, when qualifying a new source.

compliance.name: Oilfield-grade specification
compliance.desc: Drilling-grade barite must meet API 13A specific-gravity and purity specs — confirm certification before substituting a merchant-grade source into an oilfield supply chain.

compliance.name: Structural demand headwind, not a compliance flag
compliance.desc: Kaolin faces ongoing substitution pressure from cheaper calcium carbonate and talc in paper and coatings — useful context if a supplier's quote seems to be defending share rather than reflecting cost inflation.

compliance.name: Purity certification required for personal-care use
compliance.desc: Cosmetic and pharmaceutical-grade talc must carry asbestos-free certification per current testing protocols — this is a real, recurring compliance/litigation-exposure topic in North America specifically; always require current certificates of analysis, not legacy paperwork.

compliance.name: Favorable regulatory positioning vs. precipitated silica
compliance.desc: Draft EU Ecolabel criteria favor low-dust raw materials, which structurally favors pyrogenic (fumed) silica over coarser precipitated grades — a genuine tailwind, not a purchasing risk.

compliance.name: Recent bankruptcy emergence — verify current supply terms
compliance.desc: Ascend Performance Materials emerged from Chapter 11 in December 2025 — if sourcing from Ascend, confirm current contract terms, credit terms, and supply commitments reflect the post-emergence entity rather than pre-filing agreements.

compliance.name: Grade verification required for drug applications
compliance.desc: Pharmaceutical-grade PEG requires specific pharmacopeia compliance and, for PEGylation use, additional documentation on molecular-weight distribution — verify certificates of analysis match the intended regulatory pathway.

compliance.name: Regulatory tailwind, not risk
compliance.desc: Environmental rules pushing pulp mills toward elemental-chlorine-free (ECF) bleaching are a structural demand driver for sodium chlorate, not a restriction on the chemical itself.

compliance.name: Cost exposure to regional power prices
compliance.desc: Chlorate production is electrolytic and power-intensive — regional electricity price spikes pass through to chlorate cost with a short lag.

compliance.name: Palm-based supply chain scrutiny
compliance.desc: Palm-derived stearic acid faces increasing customer and regulator scrutiny (EUDR-adjacent pressure) on deforestation-linked sourcing — RSPO-certified supply commands a premium but reduces audit risk.

compliance.name: Regulatory tailwind for Ca-Zn systems
compliance.desc: REACH and equivalent global rules phasing out lead-based PVC stabilisers structurally favor zinc/calcium stearate systems — useful context, not a purchasing risk.

compliance.name: Regulatory approval is a genuine differentiator
compliance.desc: Food-contact and produce-wash uses require specific EPA/FDA approvals per formulation — verify the supplier's specific grade is cleared for your end use, not just PAA generically.

compliance.name: Handling and shelf-life constraints
compliance.desc: PAA solutions degrade over time and require careful storage; this limits substitution flexibility and favors suppliers with regional production/distribution proximity.

compliance.name: Detergent-use restrictions in some markets
compliance.desc: Several jurisdictions restrict or ban STPP in household detergents due to eutrophication concerns from phosphate wastewater discharge — verify your end-use market still permits phosphate builders before locking in long-term volume.

compliance.name: Certification required for potable water use
compliance.desc: PolyDADMAC used in drinking water treatment requires NSF/ANSI 60 certification — confirm the specific grade and dose rate quoted are covered under current certification, not just the supplier's product line generally.

compliance.name: Antimicrobial claims require registered actives
compliance.desc: Any disinfectant/sanitizer claim in the US requires an EPA-registered BAC active — unregistered technical-grade material cannot legally be marketed with biocidal claims.

compliance.name: Structural feedstock decline in Florida
compliance.desc: Florida orange production has declined significantly due to citrus greening disease, tightening d-limonene byproduct supply from that region specifically — Brazilian sourcing has partly offset this but diversifying supply regions is a legitimate risk-mitigation topic to raise.

compliance.name: Handling hazard, not a regulatory approval issue
compliance.desc: Sodium sulfide can generate toxic H2S gas on contact with acids — verify supplier packaging/handling documentation meets your site's hazardous-materials protocol, independent of price.

compliance.name: Application-method restrictions, an active regulatory topic
compliance.desc: 2,4-D formulations face ongoing regulatory attention around drift and volatility, particularly with newer low-volatility ester/choline-salt formulations designed for herbicide-tolerant crop systems — verify current label restrictions rather than assuming legacy formulation rules apply.

compliance.name: Structural regulatory tailwind
compliance.desc: EU rules favoring biodegradable, non-chlorinated bleach systems are a demand driver for sodium percarbonate, not a restriction — useful context when a supplier cites 'regulatory compliance' as a price justification.

compliance.name: Genuine, ongoing reformulation pressure
compliance.desc: Certain accelerator classes (particularly some amine-based sulfenamides) can form carcinogenic nitrosamines under specific processing conditions — this is an active reformulation topic under REACH, not a settled non-issue; ask suppliers directly about their nitrosamine-control measures.

compliance.name: Not a drop-in substitute pair
compliance.desc: AKD and ASA have different reactivity, cure time, and paper-machine-speed compatibility — a supplier proposing to switch chemistries to solve a cost or supply issue should be evaluated on paper-machine trial data, not price alone.

compliance.name: Standard latex-industry specification
compliance.desc: Residual monomer (free styrene/butadiene) limits apply to SB latex, particularly for indoor-air-quality-sensitive applications like carpet backing — request residual monomer data on the certificate of analysis.

compliance.name: Formulation-specific qualification
compliance.desc: External thermal insulation system (ETICS) formulations are typically qualified as a complete system including the specific RDP binder — switching RDP suppliers on an approved ETICS formulation may require system requalification/certification, not just a raw-material swap.

compliance.name: Genuine substitution opportunity, not a compliance risk
compliance.desc: Sodium gluconate is increasingly promoted as a biodegradable replacement for EDTA-based chelators in formulations facing environmental scrutiny — a real reformulation lever to raise with customers under sustainability pressure.

compliance.name: Regulatory driver, not a restriction
compliance.desc: Coalescents exist specifically to help formulators meet VOC regulations (e.g., EPA's January 2025 aerosol-coatings rule) — a genuine demand tailwind, not a compliance risk for the chemical itself.

compliance.flag: EU reproductive toxicant classification / US TSCA risk finding
compliance.name: Genuine regulatory restriction, not just a label
compliance.desc: NMP is classified as a category 2 developmental toxicant in the EU (non-cosmetic product use restricted to 5% concentration), and a US EPA TSCA draft risk evaluation found unreasonable risk to workers via inhalation/dermal exposure — this is a real reformulation-pressure topic, not boilerplate, and worth flagging proactively to any customer using NMP in higher concentrations.

compliance.name: Grade-specific, not a general compliance issue
compliance.desc: Electronics-grade PGMEA requires trace-metal and particulate specifications well beyond industrial grade — verify certificates of analysis explicitly state semiconductor/electronic grade if that's the intended use.

compliance.name: Grade verification is critical, not optional
compliance.desc: Electronic-grade sulfuric acid purity requirements are dramatically stricter than industrial grade (trace metal limits in the ppt range) — this is not a category where 'equivalent' industrial-grade material can substitute; always verify SEMI-grade certification.

compliance.name: Grade verification is critical, not optional
compliance.desc: As with electronic-grade sulfuric acid, purity requirements are far stricter than industrial/agricultural ammonia grades — verify SEMI-grade certification rather than assuming any 'high purity' claim is sufficient.

compliance.name: Application-specific density/purity grade
compliance.desc: Completion-fluid-grade sodium bromide requires specific density and clarity specifications distinct from general industrial grade — confirm the quoted grade matches the well-completion application.

compliance.name: Density spec is application-critical, not negotiable down
compliance.desc: High-pressure/high-temperature well completions have hard minimum density requirements — don't substitute to a lower-density brine purely for cost without engineering sign-off.

compliance.name: Service-intensive product, not a standalone commodity
compliance.desc: DRA suppliers typically provide dedicated field engineering and injection-system support as part of the product relationship — factor this service value into any total-cost comparison, not just per-liter/per-kg pricing.

compliance.name: Genuine sustainability positioning
compliance.desc: Pine oil's natural, renewable, byproduct-of-pulping origin is a legitimate sustainability differentiator versus petroleum-based solvents — useful for customers with green-sourcing requirements.

compliance.name: Genuine food-labeling requirement
compliance.desc: Sulfites are a recognized allergen requiring label declaration in food and wine products in most jurisdictions — verify the end-use application accounts for this, distinct from any supplier-quality issue.

compliance.name: Oxidizer hazmat classification
compliance.desc: Potassium permanganate is a Class 5.1 oxidizer for transport — segregation from combustibles/organics applies in storage and freight.

compliance.name: Oxidizer hazmat transport class
compliance.desc: Calcium hypochlorite is a Class 5.1 oxidizer for transport — segregation requirements from combustibles/organics apply in storage and freight, affecting logistics cost and supplier qualification.

compliance.name: Distinct supply chains, not interchangeable
compliance.desc: Pharma-grade HPMC requires substantially different purity documentation than construction-grade — this is a genuine grade split worth confirming before switching suppliers for cost reasons.

compliance.name: Regulatory filing dependency
compliance.desc: MCC used in an approved drug formulation is typically specified by brand/grade in the regulatory filing — switching suppliers for an approved product may require regulatory notification/re-validation, not just a supply-chain decision.

compliance.name: Grade verification required
compliance.desc: Pharma-grade magnesium stearate must meet pharmacopeia purity/endotoxin specs — verify certificates of analysis match the pharmacopeia cited, not just a generic 'pharma grade' claim.

compliance.name: Bovine sourcing / BSE controls
compliance.desc: Bovine-sourced gelatin requires BSE-free country-of-origin certification for EU import — porcine or fish-sourced alternatives avoid this but carry religious/dietary sourcing constraints (halal/kosher) instead.

compliance.name: Feedstock is agricultural and seasonal
compliance.desc: Pectin extraction depends on citrus peel or apple pomace supply from the juice industry — regional citrus harvest quality/yield affects pectin cost and grade availability seasonally.

compliance.name: Ongoing EFSA safety re-assessment
compliance.desc: Carrageenan (E407) has faced periodic EFSA re-evaluation attention in the EU, particularly around degraded/low-molecular-weight fractions — verify current-spec compliance rather than assuming legacy approval status.

compliance.name: Wild-harvest vs. cultivated feedstock
compliance.desc: Alginate feedstock (kelp/brown seaweed) is more commonly wild-harvested than carrageenan's cultivated red seaweed — sourcing region (Chile, Norway, China) affects both price stability and sustainability-audit exposure.

compliance.name: Clean-label pressure, not a regulatory ban
compliance.desc: Sodium benzoate (E211) faces ongoing clean-label consumer pressure and reformulation trends (especially combined with ascorbic acid, where benzene formation is a labeling concern), but remains broadly approved — treat this as a reformulation-risk conversation with customers, not a supply restriction.

compliance.name: Standard food-additive labeling, not a restriction
compliance.desc: Potassium sorbate (E202) is broadly approved with no significant current restriction pressure, unlike sodium benzoate's clean-label scrutiny — a genuine formulation advantage worth highlighting to customers navigating preservative-system reformulation.

compliance.name: Clean-label reformulation trend
compliance.desc: Many modified starches carry E14xx numbers requiring label declaration in the EU — native or physically-modified (non-chemical) starches can sometimes substitute to avoid this, a genuine reformulation lever worth raising with customers facing clean-label pressure.

compliance.name: Grade verification is critical for battery applications
compliance.desc: Battery-grade lithium hydroxide requires very tight impurity limits (particularly iron, and other transition metals) — technical-grade material cannot substitute for cathode-precursor use without requalification.

compliance.name: Application-specific grade selection
compliance.desc: PAG lubricants used in refrigeration/AC compressors must match the specific refrigerant chemistry in use — confirm compatibility rather than treating PAG as a single interchangeable product.

compliance.name: Genuine differentiator for environmentally sensitive uses
compliance.desc: Readily biodegradable ester grades (e.g., meeting OECD 301B) carry real certification requirements distinct from standard industrial ester — confirm certification if the end use requires it, since not all polyol esters qualify.

compliance.name: Ongoing regulatory attention on pyrethroids generally
compliance.desc: Pyrethroid insecticides as a class face ongoing regulatory scrutiny regarding pollinator and aquatic toxicity — verify current label restrictions rather than assuming legacy approval status is unchanged.

compliance.flag: Neonicotinoid pollinator restrictions (EU ban, other jurisdictions)
compliance.name: Significant, active regulatory restriction — more severe than the pyrethroid flag above
compliance.desc: Thiamethoxam is banned for outdoor use in the EU (since 2018) due to pollinator-toxicity concerns, and faces restrictions or review in several other jurisdictions — this is a substantive, active regulatory constraint on where and how this product can legally be sold and used, not a minor labeling issue.

compliance.name: Highly regulated, ongoing scrutiny
compliance.desc: Paraquat is a Restricted Use Pesticide in the US (certified-applicator-only) and has faced litigation and regulatory review in multiple jurisdictions over Parkinson's-disease association claims — this is an active, well-documented regulatory and reputational topic, not boilerplate.

compliance.name: Not interchangeable with MOP
compliance.desc: SOP cannot be substituted with cheaper MOP for chloride-sensitive end uses — verify the end application before entertaining a MOP-based cost-reduction proposal from a supplier.

compliance.name: Distinct grades, not interchangeable
compliance.desc: Animal feed-grade zinc sulfate requires different heavy-metal/purity certification than agricultural fertilizer-grade — confirm the certified grade matches the intended end use.

compliance.name: Emerging grade differentiation
compliance.desc: Battery-precursor-grade manganese sulfate requires substantially tighter impurity limits than agricultural fertilizer grade — as battery demand grows, expect increasing price divergence between the two grades that wasn't historically significant.

compliance.name: Not interchangeable for tire applications
compliance.desc: Highly dispersible silica (HDS) commands a real price premium over standard precipitated silica and is not a drop-in substitute for green-tire tread compounds — confirm which grade a quote covers before comparing supplier pricing.

compliance.name: Distinct grade required for food and oral-care use
compliance.desc: Food-grade and oral-care-grade precipitated silica require heavy-metal and purity certification well beyond industrial/tire grade — verify certificates of analysis match the intended end use.

compliance.name: Hazmat transport and storage classification
compliance.desc: Xanthates are classified as dangerous goods, Class 4.2 (spontaneously combustible), and can decompose into CS2 and alcohol on exposure to air/moisture or impure manufacture — verify supplier packaging, moisture-barrier integrity, and storage documentation, this is a genuine operational safety issue, not boilerplate.

compliance.name: Decomposition hazard in acidic circuits
compliance.desc: Xanthates decompose and release toxic H2S gas in highly acidic flotation circuits — a real operational constraint that also happens to be one of the reasons phosphine-based specialty collectors (see MIN-AEROPHINE-LIQ) are chosen for low-pH applications instead.

compliance.name: Manufacturing-side hazard, relevant to supply continuity
compliance.desc: Phosphine gas is highly toxic and used as a manufacturing intermediate (not present in the final product at hazardous levels) — this affects which producers can manufacture this chemistry at all and is part of why the supply base is so concentrated; relevant context for supply-continuity risk assessment, not a handling issue for the end user.

compliance.name: Genuine ESG/tailings advantage
compliance.desc: Lower toxicity and better biodegradability in tailings ponds post-use is a real, documented advantage over xanthate — a legitimate ESG/permitting talking point for mines facing tailings-discharge scrutiny, not just a marketing claim.

compliance.name: Structural supply-security risk, not a routine sourcing issue
compliance.desc: With China controlling the large majority of both fluorspar mining and HF production, any Chinese export policy shift (quotas, licensing, environmental crackdowns on fluorspar mining) can tighten global HF supply with limited near-term alternatives — treat multi-year HF contracts with China-origin material as carrying genuine geopolitical risk, not just price risk.

compliance.flag: Highly toxic / corrosive — Class 8 + inhalation hazard
compliance.name: Severe handling and transport hazard
compliance.desc: Anhydrous HF is severely corrosive and highly toxic via inhalation and skin contact (can cause systemic poisoning even from small skin exposure) — this drives real, non-negotiable requirements for supplier packaging, transport, and site-handling certification.

compliance.name: Executed geopolitical supply restriction, not theoretical
compliance.desc: China suspended exports of a wide range of rare earths in 2025 in response to US tariffs — this has already happened and directly affects global availability and pricing of magnet-grade rare earths; any NdPr sourcing strategy should explicitly address exposure to China-origin material versus the smaller, higher-cost ex-China alternatives.

compliance.flag: EU Critical Raw Materials Act / US critical minerals designation
compliance.name: Regulatory tailwind for non-China supply, not a restriction on this product
compliance.desc: Both the EU and US have designated rare earths (including NdPr) as critical raw materials, unlocking subsidy/investment support for non-China separation capacity like Solvay's La Rochelle expansion — relevant context when evaluating a supplier's expansion credibility and cost trajectory.

compliance.name: Active, executed regulatory restriction
compliance.desc: The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety reduced the permitted use concentration for ethylhexyl salicylate from 10% to 5%, requiring reformulation and retesting across a large number of existing sunscreen products — a real, already-in-effect constraint, not a pending review.

compliance.name: Environmental toxicity classification, recently triggered
compliance.desc: A recent daphnia reproduction study triggered a new CLP self-classification of ethylhexyl salicylate as Aquatic Chronic 1 — relevant to environmental discharge permitting and 'reef-safe' marketing claims.

compliance.name: Active brand-side reformulation driver
compliance.desc: Octocrylene can degrade into benzophenone (a substance with its own safety scrutiny) within finished sunscreen formulations over time — this specific degradation pathway is the stated reason for L'Oréal's 2025 EU phase-out and a live topic in ongoing ECHA environmental studies (daphnia reproduction, still ongoing).

compliance.flag: SCCS 2021 safety opinion — deemed safe at ≤10%
compliance.name: Current regulatory status, not at risk of imminent ban
compliance.desc: The EU's SCCS concluded in March 2021 that octocrylene is safe at concentrations up to 10% individually, with insufficient evidence of endocrine-disrupting effects for a human health risk assessment — brand-side reformulation away from it is a voluntary/reputational response, not a regulatory mandate.

compliance.name: Structural market concentration, not a regulatory issue
compliance.desc: The ~300 bar / >300°C synthesis conditions represent genuine, durable barriers to new entrants — this is why the market has remained a near-duopoly (BASF/Kuraray) for decades despite citral's broad downstream importance; useful context when a supplier claims capacity constraints, since credible new entrants are genuinely rare.

compliance.flag: EU anti-dumping duties on Chinese imports (90.0-115.9%, effective Dec 19 2025)
compliance.name: Major, already-executed trade policy change
compliance.desc: Any EU buyer currently sourcing choline chloride from China faces a duty increase of 90-116% effective immediately for a 5-year term — this is not a risk to monitor, it is already in effect and should be reflected in any current EU sourcing cost comparison.

compliance.flag: Dual food/feed and industrial (oilfield) grade specification
compliance.name: Distinct grades, not interchangeable
compliance.desc: Feed-grade choline chloride requires nutritional/purity certification distinct from industrial oilfield grade — confirm the certified grade matches the intended end use.

compliance.name: Grade-specific requirement, distinct from feed grade
compliance.desc: Cosmetic-grade D-panthenol requires purity and stability documentation distinct from feed-grade calcium pantothenate — confirm certification matches the intended personal-care application.

compliance.name: Grade-specific requirement, not a general compliance issue
compliance.desc: Fragrance-grade DPG requires tighter odor and aldehyde-content specifications than industrial grade, since any off-note would compromise the fragrance compound it carries — confirm grade before comparing supplier pricing.

compliance.name: Real, in-effect market-access restriction
compliance.desc: Octinoxate is banned for sale in Hawaii and Palau specifically to protect coral reef ecosystems — an already-executed market restriction requiring destination-specific formulation, not a pending review.

compliance.flag: EU Commission opinion finalized 2025 — endocrine-active but approved ≤10%
compliance.name: Review resolved, not still pending
compliance.desc: Correction to an earlier characterization of this as an open review: the European Commission finalized its opinion on octinoxate in 2025, concluding it is an endocrine-active substance but remains safe for use as a UV filter at concentrations up to 10% — current EU approval status is confirmed and settled, not pending.

compliance.flag: EU SCCS Group A review (ongoing since 2019)
compliance.name: Active review, current approval unaffected
compliance.desc: Homosalate remains part of an ongoing EU safety data review alongside three other UV filters — no restriction currently in effect, but this is a live regulatory topic to monitor, not a settled matter.

compliance.name: Formulation-specific, not a compliance risk
compliance.desc: Regulatory maximum use concentrations for ethylhexyl triazone are lower than most other UV filters (around 5%) — a formulation design constraint rather than a safety restriction.

compliance.flag: BASF force majeure event (2024), now resolved
compliance.name: Historical supply disruption, useful context for supplier risk assessment
compliance.desc: The 2024 BASF Ludwigshafen fire is a concrete, real example of single-site concentration risk in this category — even though normalized by end of 2025, it's a legitimate data point for any multi-year single-source contract risk discussion.

compliance.flag: Synthetic vs. natural sourcing distinction, EU labeling relevance
compliance.name: Genuine market segmentation, not a regulatory restriction
compliance.desc: European aquaculture increasingly specifies natural-sourced astaxanthin for premium/branded salmon programs — verify which sourcing route a quote covers, since synthetic and natural astaxanthin are not interchangeable for brands with natural-sourcing commitments even though both are approved.

compliance.flag: EFSA authorization across all animal species (recently confirmed)
compliance.name: Regulatory tailwind, not a restriction
compliance.desc: EFSA has recently confirmed authorization of 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 across all animal species, removing prior species-specific authorization gaps — a positive, expanding-use regulatory development.

compliance.flag: FDA/regulatory traceability requirements for premix ingredients
compliance.name: Increasing documentation burden, industry-wide trend
compliance.desc: Regulators have expanded traceability requirements for feed premix ingredients — expect increased documentation/audit requests from suppliers as a standard part of qualification, not an unusual ask.

compliance.name: Distinct grades with real regulatory-documentation implications
compliance.desc: Pharmaceutical-grade pyridoxine HCl requires GMP production and formal drug master file documentation (e.g. DSM-Firmenich's active China DMF) — feed-grade material from commodity Chinese producers does not carry this documentation and cannot substitute for pharma applications.

compliance.flag: Coconut/palm kernel oil feedstock sustainability sourcing
compliance.name: Feedstock-level ESG consideration, not a restriction on the finished product
compliance.desc: RSPO or equivalent sustainable-sourcing certification for the underlying palm kernel oil is an increasingly common buyer requirement — verify certification chain if sustainability claims matter for the end formulation.

compliance.flag: Coconut/palm kernel oil feedstock sustainability sourcing
compliance.name: Same feedstock-level ESG consideration as IPM
compliance.desc: RSPO or equivalent certification relevant for sustainability-conscious buyers.

compliance.name: Feedstock-level consideration
compliance.desc: Same RSPO/sustainable sourcing relevance as other coconut-derived personal care ingredients in this library.

compliance.name: Real, consequential grade separation
compliance.desc: Pharmaceutical and vaccine-grade Polysorbate 80 requires substantially higher purity and documentation than cosmetic/food-grade material — do not substitute one for the other; this is a genuine safety-relevant distinction, not just a pricing tier.

compliance.name: Structural demand tailwind, not a restriction on this product itself
compliance.desc: This product carries no direct regulatory restriction — its growth is a direct consequence of restrictions on the silicone chemistry it's replacing.

compliance.name: Certification-driving demand factor
compliance.desc: This ingredient's bio-based status is specifically relevant to Ecocert and similar natural-cosmetics certification requirements — a genuine certification-compliance driver, not just a marketing angle.

compliance.flag: Rapeseed oil feedstock sourcing (high-erucic variety specifically)
compliance.name: Feedstock-specific sourcing note
compliance.desc: Behenic acid derives specifically from high-erucic rapeseed oil, a distinct agricultural variety from standard canola — relevant context for feedstock availability discussions.

compliance.name: Same molecule, different grade requirements
compliance.desc: Salicylic acid is also the direct precursor to aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) — pharmaceutical-grade material requires distinct purity documentation from cosmetic-grade; confirm grade matches intended use.

compliance.name: Route-specific quality consideration
compliance.desc: Material produced via the chloroacetic acid route requires verification of residual chlorinated byproduct levels — a genuine quality-control distinction between the two production routes, not merely a sourcing preference.

compliance.name: Severe, well-established health hazard
compliance.desc: Benzene is a confirmed human carcinogen with strict occupational exposure limits globally — transport, storage, and handling carry significant regulatory documentation requirements independent of any specific formulation use.

compliance.flag: Extremely reactive, flammable, and carcinogenic gas
compliance.name: Severe handling/transport hazard, integrated-production norm
compliance.desc: EO's extreme reactivity and toxicity mean it is rarely transported far from its production site — most commercial supply chains are built around integrated on-site downstream conversion rather than merchant EO shipment.

compliance.flag: Toxic, flammable liquid — strict handling requirements
compliance.name: Standard severe-hazard chemical handling
compliance.desc: Acrylonitrile is toxic via inhalation and skin contact and requires strict handling/transport documentation, consistent with its classification as a hazardous industrial chemical.

compliance.flag: Corrosive, inhibited monomer — requires stabilizer management
compliance.name: Standard reactive-monomer handling requirement
compliance.desc: Acrylic acid is shipped with polymerization inhibitors and requires temperature-controlled storage to prevent uncontrolled polymerization — a standard but non-trivial handling requirement for any buyer new to monomer sourcing.

compliance.name: Standard hazardous-chemical handling
compliance.desc: Phenol causes severe skin/eye burns and is toxic if absorbed — standard industrial handling documentation applies.

compliance.flag: Endocrine disruptor concerns — active regulatory scrutiny
compliance.name: Ongoing global regulatory review, some restrictions already in effect
compliance.desc: BPA faces active regulatory restriction in food-contact applications in several jurisdictions (EU, others) due to endocrine-disruption concerns — verify current application-specific restrictions before assuming approval.

compliance.name: Route-specific environmental consideration
compliance.desc: The chlorohydrin route (modeled here) generates chlorinated organic byproducts requiring treatment, unlike the newer HPPO route — relevant context if evaluating a specific producer's environmental profile.

compliance.flag: Uses HCN (hydrogen cyanide) as a process intermediate
compliance.name: Manufacturing-side hazard relevant to producer qualification
compliance.desc: The ACH route requires HCN as an intermediate — extremely toxic, relevant to which producers can manufacture this chemistry safely at scale, not a hazard present in the finished MMA product itself.

compliance.name: Genuine safety-relevant end use, not incidental
compliance.desc: Pentaerythritol's role in intumescent (fire-retardant) coatings is a genuine safety-critical application — relevant context for understanding demand stability in this specific niche even during general construction downturns.

compliance.name: Structural regulatory/consumer tailwind, not a restriction on this product
compliance.desc: This product benefits directly from regulatory and consumer pressure against traditional phthalate plasticizers — a positive driver, not a compliance risk.

compliance.flag: Possible human carcinogen (IARC Group 2A/2B, varies by assessment)
compliance.name: Ongoing scrutiny, standard industrial handling applies
compliance.desc: Styrene faces some carcinogenicity classification scrutiny (assessments vary by body and have shifted over time) — standard occupational exposure limit compliance applies regardless of the specific classification status at any given time.

compliance.name: Pricing behavior fundamentally different from most commodities in this library
compliance.desc: Unlike most petrochemical intermediates with relatively stable margin ranges, butadiene margins are structurally volatile because of its co-product economics — any cost model or budget forecast using a single fixed margin assumption for butadiene should be treated with more caution than for other products in this library.

compliance.flag: Battery-grade purity specification, distinct from industrial grade
compliance.name: Real, consequential grade separation
compliance.desc: Battery electrolyte applications require far stricter purity (trace metal content, moisture control) than industrial-grade ethylene carbonate — confirm grade explicitly, as this is not a minor quality tier difference but a fundamentally different qualification bar.

compliance.flag: Battery-grade purity specification, distinct from general solvent grade
compliance.name: Same grade-separation consideration as ethylene carbonate
compliance.desc: Confirm grade explicitly when sourcing for battery applications specifically — general-solvent-grade material does not meet battery electrolyte purity requirements.

compliance.name: Distinct grades, not interchangeable on cost alone
compliance.desc: Explosives-grade material has different impurity tolerances (and typically lower cost) than cosmetic/pharma-grade sorbitan monooleate — verify grade before assuming a mining-sector price applies to a personal-care sourcing question, or vice versa.

compliance.flag: Explosives transport, storage, and handling licensing
compliance.name: Severe, heavily regulated hazard class
compliance.desc: Bulk emulsion explosives require explosives-specific transport licensing, magazine storage certification, and blaster certification for use — regulatory compliance here is far more stringent than for any other mining reagent in this library, reflecting the product's inherent hazard.

compliance.name: Genuine security regulation, not boilerplate
compliance.desc: Many jurisdictions impose specific security and reporting controls on ammonium nitrate-based explosives given historical misuse as improvised explosives — verify current supplier/buyer licensing status, this is an active compliance area, not a settled formality.

compliance.name: Standard corrosive-liquid hazmat classification
compliance.desc: Glacial acetic acid is corrosive and requires standard hazmat transport/handling documentation.

compliance.name: Genuine, established regulatory concern
compliance.desc: Aniline carries carcinogenicity concerns and strict occupational exposure limits — standard hazmat/toxicity documentation applies.

compliance.name: Standard reactive-chemical handling
compliance.desc: Acetic anhydride reacts vigorously with water and is corrosive — standard hazmat handling and moisture-controlled storage apply.

compliance.name: Active regulatory topic for open-mold composite fabrication
compliance.desc: Styrene emissions from open-mold UPR composite fabrication (marine, tanks) face increasing air-quality/worker-exposure regulation in several jurisdictions — a genuine, ongoing compliance topic for composite fabricators specifically.

compliance.name: Genuine, established regulatory concern, parallels NMP
compliance.desc: DMF carries reproductive toxicity classifications similar to NMP (already flagged in this library) — standard exposure-limit and handling documentation applies, this is an active workplace-safety topic, not boilerplate.

compliance.name: Genuine, established regulatory concern
compliance.desc: ECH carries carcinogenicity classification and strict occupational exposure limits — standard hazmat/toxicity documentation applies.

compliance.name: Same regulatory context as HEDP/ATMP
compliance.desc: Phosphonates face similar wastewater-discharge scrutiny to phosphate builders (STPP, already in this library) in some jurisdictions — verify current local regulatory status before large-volume commitments.

compliance.name: Same regulatory context as the rest of this phosphonate family
compliance.desc: Same wastewater-discharge scrutiny considerations as HEDP/ATMP/DTPMP apply.

compliance.name: Standard severe-hazard chemical handling
compliance.desc: Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidizer and highly corrosive — standard hazmat transport/handling documentation applies.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard coatings dispersant chemistry — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Acrylic/maleic copolymer dispersants carry no major known regulatory restriction; the underlying acrylic acid and maleic anhydride feedstocks are standard, REACH-registered petrochemicals.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard mineral-oil defoamer — no acute regulatory flag
compliance.desc: Mineral-oil-based defoamer emulsions carry no major known regulatory restriction and are the lower-VOC-impact defoamer choice relative to some solvent-carried alternatives.

compliance.flag: Alkylphenol-ethoxylate-adjacent chemistry under periodic EU scrutiny, but chemically distinct from restricted NPE/OPE
compliance.name: TSPE is not the same restricted substance class as nonylphenol/octylphenol ethoxylates
compliance.desc: Nonylphenol ethoxylates (NPE) and octylphenol ethoxylates (OPE) are restricted in the EU (REACH Annex XVII) for aquatic-toxicity and endocrine-disruption concerns; tristyrylphenol ethoxylate (TSPE) uses a styrene-derived hydrophobe rather than the nonyl/octyl-phenol structure specifically targeted by those restrictions, but as an alkylphenol-ethoxylate-adjacent chemistry it remains a substance class worth monitoring as EU alkylphenol scrutiny evolves.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Established, widely-used mild amphoteric surfactant
compliance.desc: Amphoacetates are long-established, well-characterized cosmetic and household-product ingredients with no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Favorable low-VOC, non-toxic profile — a genuinely positive regulatory position
compliance.desc: Dibasic ester solvents are non-CMR, readily biodegradable, and classified as low-VOC/non-VOC under EU Directive 1999/13/EC and equivalent US regulations — a favorable position relative to the NMP and chlorinated/aromatic solvents they are marketed to replace.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Established, widely-used nonionic surfactant chemistry
compliance.desc: EO/PO block copolymers are long-established, well-characterized nonionic surfactants with no major known regulatory restriction.

compliance.name: Phosphorus trichloride is a Chemical Weapons Convention Schedule 3 chemical
compliance.desc: PCl3, a key manufacturing intermediate, is listed under CWC Schedule 3 — its procurement and storage are subject to declaration requirements and end-use certificates in most jurisdictions. This constrains which producers can manufacture phosphinic acid extractants and contributes to the concentrated supply base.

compliance.name: Strategic reagent for battery-metal and critical-mineral extraction
compliance.desc: As the dominant Co/Ni separation reagent and an emerging lithium DLE extractant, CYANEX 272/936P is a chokepoint in the battery-metals supply chain — security-of-supply considerations are driving some mining companies and sovereign funds to seek multi-source alternatives.

compliance.name: Nonylphenol feedstock under EU REACH SVHC
compliance.desc: The nonylphenol starting material for hydroxyoxime synthesis is an EU REACH SVHC and subject to authorization — while it is consumed during synthesis (not present in the final reagent), supply chain availability and cost of nonylphenol feedstock are affected by regulatory pressure, potentially tightening feedstock supply for European-based manufacturing.

compliance.name: Kerosene diluent contributes to on-site VOC emissions
compliance.desc: The reagent is supplied dissolved in high-flash-point kerosene; on-site VOC emissions from SX circuits are regulated under mine environmental permits. Not a product compliance issue per se but affects total site emissions budget.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard food/fragrance ingredient — GRAS, FEMA-listed
compliance.desc: Vanillin is FDA-GRAS, FEMA 3107, EU-approved flavoring substance (FL-no 05.018). No acute regulatory restrictions on synthetic vanillin in any major market.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard industrial amine — widely used in cosmetics and construction
compliance.desc: TEA has no major regulatory restriction. It is listed in the EU Cosmetics Regulation Annex III with concentration limits (max 2.5% in leave-on products). GRAS for incidental food contact.

compliance.flag: DEA classified as potential nitrosamine precursor
compliance.name: Cosmetic and food-contact regulatory scrutiny
compliance.desc: DEA can react with nitrosating agents to form NDEA (N-nitrosodiethanolamine), a suspected carcinogen. EU Cosmetics Regulation limits DEA in cosmetic products. Not a manufacturing ban but affects downstream formulation choices.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard industrial alcohol
compliance.desc: 2-Ethylhexanol has no significant regulatory restriction. Downstream DEHP plasticizer faces REACH Annex XIV authorization requirement, but 2-EH itself is unrestricted.

compliance.flag: Acrylamide monomer is classified as a probable human carcinogen (IARC Group 2A)
compliance.name: CMR substance — strict handling/exposure controls required
compliance.desc: Acrylamide monomer is classified Carc. 1B, Muta. 1B, Repr. 2 under CLP/GHS. Polymerized PAM is non-hazardous, but monomer handling requires strict exposure controls. EU REACH restricts residual monomer in consumer products to <0.1%.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard inorganic salt — no regulatory restriction
compliance.desc: Calcium chloride has no significant regulatory restriction. Food-grade CaCl₂ is GRAS (FDA) and E509 (EU).

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Refinery product — standard hydrocarbon handling
compliance.desc: Naphtha is a standard refinery product with no specific regulatory restriction beyond normal flammable liquid handling requirements.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Foundational petrochemical — no restriction
compliance.desc: Propylene has no regulatory restriction. Standard industrial handling as a flammable gas.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Foundational petrochemical — no restriction
compliance.desc: Ethylene itself has no regulatory restriction. Downstream products (VCM, EO) face their own regulatory scrutiny.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Standard industrial intermediate
compliance.desc: BDO has no major regulatory restriction. Downstream product GBL is a controlled substance in some jurisdictions but BDO itself is not.

compliance.flag: No significant compliance or substitution concern identified
compliance.name: Mature industrial chemical — transport/handling regulated but not restricted
compliance.desc: Chlorine gas is hazardous (toxic, oxidizer) and subject to strict transport/storage regulations, but it is not subject to REACH restriction or phase-out. The industry transitioned away from mercury-cell technology under EU regulation.
